extracted.intended_audience: secondary mathematics educators, curriculum developers, and mathematics education researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and organizing high-school mathematics curricula around general and mathematics-specific 'habits of mind' so students acquire mathematical ways of thinking rather than only topical facts. The page lists specific habits and mathematical approaches with examples and implementation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize curriculum around habits of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Design the curriculum to develop students' mathematical habits of mind (general thinking habits and content-specific mathematical approaches) rather than to chase particular fashionable topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus instruction and course/sequence design on giving students experience with the methods mathematicians use (conjecturing, experimenting, abstraction, etc.), so what students learn is robust to changing technical content. Use habits as the organizer: include repeated problem types and tasks that cultivate these habits across courses. The article argues this approach reduces the risk of curricula becoming obsolete and better prepares students for future mathematical/technological needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students Should Be Pattern Sniffers
rubrics_metrics.description: Foster delight and habit of looking for regularities and patterns in numbers, data, and situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to search for shortcuts, regularities (e.g., primes that are sums of two squares, divisibility tests), and to pose pattern-driven problems for themselves. Make pattern-finding central to posed problems and student-generated tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students Should Be Experimenters
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage students to perform experiments (numerical, graphical, algorithmic), vary parameters, hold variables constant, and use thought experiments as first steps toward insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make experimentation a routine response to problems: try small/large values, change one parameter at a time, record results, and use experiments to suggest conjectures. Also teach skepticism about empirical results and the limitations of experimental discovery; experimental results should motivate but not replace theoretical justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students Should Be Describers
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop students' ability to give precise descriptions of processes, invent notation, argue convincingly, and write mathematical explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create classroom norms where students describe steps, produce written and oral explanations, invent useful notation when needed, and trade explanations with classmates. Emphasize that describing 'what you do' is central to understanding and that writing and presentation should be practiced regularly as part of mathematical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students Should Be Tinkerers
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage the habit of taking mathematical objects, procedures, or models apart and reassembling them to see what happens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide tasks where students alter sequences of operations (e.g., compositions of transformations), intentionally break or modify definitions, and explore consequences of 'mistakes' rather than discarding them. Promote curiosity about variant constructions and their outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students Should Be Inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Enable students to invent mathematics: rules for games, algorithms, explanations, or axioms that arise from attempts to model or clarify situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support invention that is internally consistent and motivated by experience (not arbitrary). Use concrete problems (e.g., haggling example leading to binary operation a ⊙ b = (a + 2b)/3) to show how inventing definitions and systems emerges from trying to model phenomena. Encourage seeking isomorphisms between structures as part of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students Should Be Visualizers
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate multiple kinds of visualization: picturing objects/processes mentally, constructing visual analogues (area models, geometric models), and creating visual accompaniments for nonvisual processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have students construct drawings, graphs, tables, and models (2D/3D) to support thinking; use visualization to aid mental arithmetic, estimation, and to think of processes as machines (input-output). Teach a repertoire of visual metaphors (Venn diagrams, factor trees, geometric pictures) and encourage using visualization where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students Should Be Conjecturers
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop the habit of forming plausible conjectures grounded in evidence and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage conjecturing based on experiments but require that conjectures be tied to evidence and to attempts at justification. Use iterative activities (e.g., running many experiments with a Logo procedure) to show how conjectures emerge and how deeper conjectures require analysis beyond mere pattern observation. Provide examples of weak vs deeper conjectures to scaffold students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students Should Be Guessers
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote guessing and working backward as productive research strategies to get familiar with problems and generate approximations or insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to check and refine guesses, use guessing to find closer approximations, and to leverage the process of checking guesses as a way to discover new strategies and problem structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians Talk Big and Think Small
rubrics_metrics.description: Train students to translate general abstract statements into concrete special cases and collections of examples as a route to understanding and theory building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make moving between general statements and concrete examples routine: when given an abstract theorem, practice producing many concrete instances; when faced with problems, show how special cases illuminate general behavior. Use this habit to build intuition that leads to theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians Talk Small and Think Big
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach students to see how very simple problems can lead to deep theories and how complex theories often arise from small examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use modest concrete problems (e.g., sum-of-two-squares) as entry points to larger abstractions (Gaussian integers) and show that abstraction and generalization often originate from studying and amplifying simple cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians Use Functions (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize the centrality of functions as a unifying idea in mathematics: using operations that transform objects and thinking of relations as mappings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Help students view mathematical processes as functions and to use the functional viewpoint as a translator between different perspectives (geometric, algebraic, analytic). The article subdivides uses into algorithms, dependencies, and mappings (see three specific entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians Use Functions — Algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use functions to describe algorithms: sets of repeated steps that transform inputs to outputs and reveal coherence in calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to express iterative or recursive processes as functions/algorithms, show how algorithms capture patterns and provide calculational shortcuts, and present inductively defined algorithms (e.g., extended Euclidean algorithm) with worked examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians Use Functions — Dependencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Use functions to describe dependencies among quantities (analytic viewpoint), especially continuous or causal variations (e.g., physics, mechanics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include tasks where students model how one quantity depends on another (rate, time, causal change) and use analytic thinking to study these dependencies as functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians Use Functions — Mappings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mappings (combinatorial viewpoint) to translate between sets or structures to aid counting and correspondences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach constructions of correspondences between well-understood sets and less-understood ones (bijections, injections) as a counting and structural tool; use mappings to reduce unfamiliar problems to known ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians Use Multiple Points of View
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage thinking about the same object via several perspectives (algebraic, geometric, analytic, combinatorial) and switching between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities that ask students to re-express problems in different languages (e.g., view complex numbers algebraically, geometrically, via functions) and illustrate how new results can emerge from changing viewpoint. Promote equipping the same set with different structures as a teaching strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians Mix Deduction and Experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach that mathematical inquiry often involves a blend of experiment (exploration, data) and deduction (proof), with proof serving to establish logical connections and suggest further results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position proof as integral to investigation (not an add-on): use experiments to generate conjectures and proofs to connect conjectures to known results, showing proofs both explain and lead to new theorems. Use classroom tasks where students develop proofs alongside experimental work (e.g., cake-cutting example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians Push the Language
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop the habit of extending and refining mathematical language and definitions to make results apply in new situations (e.g., extending exponent rules, assuming objects to derive contradictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to push definitions, invent terminology, and consider hypothetical objects (assume existence to derive contradictions) as ways to clarify and generalize mathematics. Use examples where extending language yields fruitful interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians Use Intellectual Chants
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and cultivate the ruminative, repetitive mental rehearsals mathematicians use (internal 'chants' of ideas, calculations, and partial arguments) to incubate breakthroughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make space for and describe the mental ruminations that occur during problem solving; include short descriptions of such processes in instruction to normalize extended thinking and repetition as productive practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraists Like Algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Value algorithms as recipes for solving classes of problems: many algebraic methods capture recursive or inductive processes whose descriptions are themselves mathematical objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach algorithmic thinking: present algorithms for solving equations, manipulating polynomials, finding gcds, and use worked examples to show how algorithms compress lengthy calculation and reveal structure. Include iterative computation examples (e.g., polynomial constructions, lock-combination counting) to build familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraists Break Things Into Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use decomposition theorems and the identification of 'building blocks' (e.g., prime factorization, cyclic components) to understand and analyze algebraic structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include instruction on canonical decompositions (fundamental theorem of arithmetic, decomposition of groups/vector spaces) and design tasks that have students seek and use decompositions to solve counting and structural problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraists Extend Things
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage studying objects by embedding them into larger systems (extensions) to see how properties behave and to simplify problems by changing context (e.g., integers → Gaussian integers, mod arithmetic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to enlarge the domain of study to reveal behavior (which primes split in Gaussian integers) or to remove troublesome elements by working modulo n. Use extension as a strategic tool to generate meaningful questions and tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraists Represent Things
rubrics_metrics.description: Use representations of mathematical objects by better-understood structures (e.g., coordinates, matrices) to gain algebraic perspectives on geometric or other problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide tasks that require representing points, transformations, or abstract algebraic objects concretely (ordered tuples, matrices) and practice translating between representations. Highlight representation as a research technique with many classical examples (linear algebra, group representations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare students for future technological and disciplinary change
rubrics_metrics.description: Design curricula to develop habits of mind that let students use, understand, critique, and modify technologies and systems that do not yet exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize transferable thinking skills (pattern recognition, modeling, invention, abstraction) so students can adapt to novel domains. Use habits-of-mind-centered tasks to serve both students who will pursue advanced mathematics and those who will apply mathematical thinking in other fields (journalism, diagnostics, computing).
